Am I required to carry it?

Whether you must carry flood insurance depends on your exact address and loan — look your address up on FEMA's flood map. The rule: a federally backed mortgage on a building in a high-risk zone (a Special Flood Hazard Area) legally requires it. For context, 76.3% of Nassau County's existing NFIP policies sit in those high-risk (A/V) zones — not 76.3% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

  • Zone AE30,267 policy units
  • Zone X9,650 policy units
  • Zone VE1,106 policy units
  • Zone C143 policy units
  • Zone AO90 policy units
  • Zone A0416 policy units
  • Zone A0511 policy units
  • Zone A10 policy units
  • Other or unclassified zones15 policy units

Zone mix by policy units (summed policyCount). Federal rule: a lender must require flood insurance on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a federally backed loan (42 U.S.C. §4012a). This is the mix of existing policies, not of all buildings, and does not establish any one property's obligation.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Floods don't stop at the zone line: 26.8% of the NFIP claim dollars paid in Nassau County went to policies rated outside the mapped high-risk (A/V) zone. Being outside a Special Flood Hazard Area lowers the odds and drops the federal requirement — it does not mean zero risk. (Insured claims only, by each policy's rated zone.)

How much does it cost here?

Among existing single-family primary-residence NFIP policies in Nassau County, the median annual cost is $1,470, with the middle half between $1,080 and $2,015 (30,218 policies). This is what current policyholders pay — a new policy on a different building can differ. Most policyholders here pay below FEMA's full “risk-based” price — what a policy would cost without today's discounts and yearly caps, about $1,811 median — the gap a bill can climb toward over time; see below.

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus fees), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half (p25–p75); the orange line is FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $9,976,988,000 of building and $2,488,531,000 of contents coverage across all Nassau County policies.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Flood damage is almost never covered by a standard homeowners policy; you buy flood insurance separately through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Two facts change your timing and your limits:

  • Waiting period~30 days
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most NFIP policies take effect 30 days after you buy, so you can't buy today and be covered for a storm this week — a flood-zone letter or an approaching season is a reason to act now. (Exceptions: no wait when coverage is required to close a loan, or one day after a map change puts a home in a high-risk zone.) NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents (contents bought separately); higher-value homes add private “excess” flood insurance. To buy: call the NFIP at 1-877-336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent — NFIP's price is set federally, so it is the same whichever agent you use.

Source: FEMA National Flood Insurance Program — waiting period, coverage limits and how to buy, via FloodSmart.gov. Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

40.1% of 30,218 single-family policies pay less than FEMA's own full-risk price; the median full-risk premium is $1,811 versus the $1,470 actually charged.

  • Median charged now$1,470
  • Median full-risk price$1,811
  • Pay below full risk40.1% of 30,218

Years to the full-risk price: under the statutory cap, premiums for most primary residences rise at most 18% a year (HFIAA cap, FEMA Risk Rating 2.0). At that maximum rate a policy at today's median ($1,470) would take at least about 2 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk price ($1,811). This is the cap on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy; statutory surcharges and fees are outside the cap.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How much flood risk is here?

FEMA rates Nassau County's coastal flood risk Very High and inland flood risk Relatively High — how this county compares with others, not odds for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskVery High
  • Inland flood riskRelatively High

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. coastal: expected annual flood loss above about 86% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $24,281,057 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. inland: expected annual flood loss above about 18% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $183,887,235 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Any loss figure is a whole-county estimate across all buildings, never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Between 1978 and 2026, Nassau County had 51,523 NFIP flood claims, which paid $2,258,683,594 in total.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($1,987,012,692), 2011 ($133,614,690), 1992 ($37,743,652). Net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 51,523 claims since 1978 against 41,308 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Of 51,523 NFIP flood claims ever filed in Nassau County, the average paid claim came to $51,118, and 13.6% were closed with no payment.

  • Average paid claim$51,118
  • Closed with no payment13.6%
  • Claims that paid44,513

"Closed without payment" is not the same as "denied" — it includes claims below the deductible, withdrawn, or duplicate filings. Average is over claims that paid something; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective 2026-10-25; retrieved 2026-10-25. FEMA NFIP paid-claim records. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How often has it actually flooded here?

NOAA logged 192 flood, flash-flood or coastal-flood events in Nassau County from 1996-2025, with about $19,229,500 in reported property damage.

  • Flood events logged192
  • Reported property damage$19,229,500

Physical flood events recorded by the National Weather Service for this county (1996 on), separate from insured NFIP claims — it counts floods that happened, insured or not. Damage figures are NWS field estimates, not audited, and undercount in early years.

Source: NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database. Data effective 1996-2025; retrieved 2026-10-25.

How often do the same homes flood here?

FEMA has recorded 5,387 properties in Nassau County that flooded more than once and drew federal disaster aid for repeat flood losses.

  • Repeat-loss properties5,387

FEMA-designated repetitive-loss (RL) and severe repetitive-loss (SRL) properties — individual homes with more than one flood loss over time, aggregated to the county and distinct from the annual NFIP claim counts above. A high count means the same homes flood again and again here. These drew FEMA Individual Assistance (for uninsured losses), so read it as a chronic-flooding signal, not an insured-claims total.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective 2026-10-24; retrieved 2026-10-24. FEMA repetitive-loss flood-property records. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

More data: FEMA disaster aid & reconciliation

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

FEMA approved $286,259,123 in Individual & Households housing help to Nassau County homeowners across 4 disasters, on 62,041 valid registrations.

FEMA Individual Assistance is disaster aid, usually capped and partial — separate from NFIP insurance and not a substitute for a policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective owner registrations by disaster; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the API's own totals.

In-force count: 41,308 policy units (from 37,934 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA official reconciliation count pending for this county. Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 37934/37934 fetched; claims: 51523/51523 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why premiums are rising — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
